notes.meaning: God graciously calls Jonah a second time, restoring him to his work as a prophet. Jonah is commanded to travel to the great city of Nineveh and announce the exact message God will give him. The renewal of this call shows that God had fully pardoned Jonah's past rebellion and still intended to reach the city.

Jonah sets out immediately and travels to Nineveh in complete obedience to the Lord. The city was so enormous that it took three full days just to walk through it and deliver the message. Jonah's prompt action shows that God's discipline had softened his heart and replaced his former fear with faith.

Jonah enters the city and proclaims that Nineveh will be destroyed in forty days. This time limit gave the people space to consider their ways and turn back to God before disaster struck. The warning was severe, yet the delay held out an unspoken hope for mercy.

The people of Nineveh take the warning to heart and place their faith in God's word. To express their deep sorrow for their sins, people from every walk of life declare a fast and put on rough cloth. Their rapid change of heart stood as a challenge to Israel, who often refused to listen to God's prophets.

The news reaches the king of Nineveh, and he immediately steps down from his royal throne. He takes off his fine robes, dresses in rough cloth, and sits in the dust to humble himself before the Lord. His personal grief set an example for his entire nation.

The king and his leaders issue an order that every person and domestic animal must fast without food or water. Everyone is directed to wear mourning clothes, pray earnestly, and stop their evil deeds and violent acts. Involving the herds showed how desperate the crisis was and gave outward proof of deep sorrow.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see the king's order for cattle and sheep to fast and wear sackcloth as intentional satire and humor, arguing the book is a theological parable rather than literal history.

notes.meaning: The king realizes that God is not obligated to spare them, but he hopes that the Lord will choose to be merciful. He urges the people to turn away from sin in case God relents and holds back His fiery anger. Sincere repentance always leans on the hope of God's grace.

God looks upon their actions and sees that they have truly turned away from their wicked behavior. Because they repented in heart and deed, He shows them mercy and does not destroy the city. God always welcomes people who genuinely turn from their sin.

differ.view: God's eternal decree never changes; His warning was an outward threat intended to produce repentance, altering His outward dealings without any change in His eternal mind.
God's warnings of judgment are genuinely conditional on human behavior, so He truly changed His stated purpose when the Ninevites turned away from sin.
God genuinely responds to human prayer and repentance by changing His heart toward sinners, without undermining His unchanging, faithful character.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient church teachers noted that the Ninevites pleased God and received salvation through humble prayer, even though they were outsiders to the covenant.
